title: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And the great advantage of such an experimental approach is that it does not require one to know in advance exactly what kinds of behavior can occur.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “How the Discoveries in This Chapter Were Made” (from p. 108), p. 108. Scope: methodology of studying simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-22: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Publication histories provide some evidence that computational exploration preceded unexpected findings. They do not cleanly establish what a traditional counterfactual method would have missed, so only proxies are presently resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare preregistered discovery tasks in which researchers freely explore executable systems versus construct systems targeting predefined behaviors, measuring blinded novelty and precision judgments. Existing historical cases can test a proxy, though a clean comparison would require new experiments.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical comparisons are confounded by topic and era.

Genuinely unexpected is observer-dependent.

The strongest causal test would require new researcher-participant data.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram is recommending a method and describing its advantage: experiments on fully specified programs can reveal behavior one did not set out to construct. That is a conceptual claim about inquiry. Historical episodes in the book illustrate it, but they do not supply a measurement that would confirm or refute the general advantage over constructing examples of predefined behavior.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim is about a method's ability to find phenomena that were not anticipated and to do so with mathematical precision. Whether a given discovery was 'genuinely unexpected' is a judgment about prior beliefs, not a variable in a dataset, so no confirming or refuting result is fixed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Precision of a computer experiment is a property of its specification, not an empirical outcome that distinguishes the methodology from rivals.

Any historical discovery can be redescribed as having been anticipated or as having been missed by the traditional method.
